title: Cash flow statement and free cash flow
objectives: Read the three sections of a cash flow statement.
Compute free cash flow and test earnings against cash.
body_md:
## Three sections

| Section | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Operating (CFO)** | Cash from customers less operating payments, after working-capital changes and tax |
| **Investing (CFI)** | Capex, acquisitions, sale of investments |
| **Financing (CFF)** | Borrowings and repayments, share issues, buybacks, dividends |

## From profit to cash (indirect method)

CFO = PAT + non-cash charges (depreciation) ± change in working capital ± other items.

Rising receivables and inventory **absorb cash** even when profit is strong.

## Free cash flow

**FCF = CFO − capex.** It is the cash left for lenders, owners and growth. **FCFF** adds back after-tax interest if CFO is after interest; **FCFE** is what remains for shareholders after debt flows.

## Tests that matter

- **Cash conversion** = CFO ÷ EBITDA (or PAT). Persistently below about 70–80% needs an explanation.
- Compare **cumulative CFO with cumulative PAT** over 3 to 5 years.
- Capex far above depreciation signals growth or an underinvesting past.

## Link to valuation

DCF discounts **free cash flows**, not accounting profit.

> **Exam tip:** Profit can be managed; cash is harder to fake. Growing profit with shrinking CFO is a red flag.
example: PAT ₹100, depreciation ₹30, working capital build-up ₹40: CFO is ₹90. Capex ₹50 leaves FCF of ₹40.
say: Profit is rising; I want to see the cash behind it.
Free cash flow is operating cash less capex.
never: Profit and cash flow are the same thing.
